35. Powers of the arbitral tribunal in case of default of the parties.—(1) The parties shall be free to agree on the powers of the arbitral tribunal in case of a party's failure to do anything necessary for the proper and expeditious conduct of the arbitration. 

 6. It is against this backdrop that the Respondent No. 1 issued a notice of arbitration dated 29-4-2021 which was received by the Petitioner on 5-5-2021. Thereafter, the Petitioner replied to the said notice on 19-6-2021 pursuant to which the current sole arbitrator was appointed. This led the Respondent No. 1 to file Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 2021 under section 7A of the Act before the District Judge Court. Chattogram praying for an order of status quo in relation to distributorship service operations under various heads but covering too inter alio Bayazid Bostami and Halishahar areas till disposal of the arbitration and to secure too during such period the currency of the Agreement against any potential move of the Petitioner to terminate the same till disposal of the arbitration. The District Judge accordingly passed an ad interim order of status quo dated 5-5-2021. 

 8. Thereafter on 21-11-2021, vide Order No. 14 passed in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 2021, the District Judge, Chattogram decided to extend the order of status quo until such time as Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 (filed by the Respondent No. 1 to secure the appointment of an arbitrator) was disposed of with a view to avoiding conflicting outcomes being arrived at in these two cases. Here the Petitioner contends that Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 in effect came to an end once the sole arbitrator entered appearance in the arbitration proceedings under consideration. 

 11. The hearing consequently took place on 26-1-2022 where the Petitioner's counsel emphasized that when in an arbitration the claimant fails to submit the statement of claim within time as decided by the arbitrator the Act mandates the termination of the arbitration proceedings without conferring any discretion on the tribunal to decide otherwise. It was further emphasized that in view of the District Judge's order dated 21-11-2021 in Arbitration Misc. Case No. 128 of 2021, there is no order of status quo current at that time since Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 had came to an end owing to assumption of responsibilities by the sole arbitrator. 

 13. Here, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam, as aided by the learned Advocate Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam, submits that the sole arbitrator decided not to terminate the arbitration proceedings despite his mandate under the Act to do so on the indefensible ground that the word "shall" does not necessarily have the connotation of mandatoriness attached to it but can instead have a certain element of laxity attached to it if need be. Here, Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam emphatically argues that there are numerous precedents in support of the rule of statutory interpretation that when the meaning of a word is unambiguous and clear, it should be given its ordinary and natural meaning and that this is one such case where that cardinal rule holds true. The meaning of the words of section 35(2)(a) read with section 29(1) of the Act in that sense is submitted to be clear and unambiguous, thereby, not requiring any exceptional explanation or interpretation as provided by the sole arbitrator in the present instance. Accordingly, the Petitioner views the act of the sole arbitrator not to terminate the arbitration proceedings as a clear example of bias on his part necessitating such a decision to be declared by this Court as wholly out of jurisdiction. As such, the Petitioner would also have the Arbitrator declared as consequentially having no jurisdiction to preside over the arbitration proceedings further to the Order Nos. 6 and 7 being declared as been made without jurisdiction. 

 14. The first aspect of the case taken up for consideration by this Court pertains to Order No. 6 dated 31-1-2022 of the sole arbitrator in which the Petitioner challenges the jurisdiction of the arbitrator to reject the application of the Petitioner to terminate the arbitration proceedings involving the Petitioner and the Respondent No. 1 on the grounds that "the word 'shall' does not always necessarily mean mandatory and may is not always interpreted to be directory or discretionary". 

 15. By reference to the Application and submissions made by the Petitioner's learned Advocate Mr. Tanbjib-ul Alam aided by Mr. Kazi Ershadul Alam this Court has taken particular note of the interplay of sections 29(1) and 35(2)(a) of the Act. Indeed, this Court accepts the fact that the cardinal rule of statutory interpretation applicable and attracted to this case is that when the meaning of a word is unambiguous and clear it should be given its ordinary and natural meaning and that in the circumstances the word "shall" as appears in both sections 29 and 35(2)(a) will be taken to mean mandatory. It has not also escaped this Court's attention that the Respondent No. 1 has sought to interpret the provisions of the Act in light of the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 without pinpointing the fact that there are some material differences in the provisions of these two pieces of legislation. Section 25 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides for a determination of a defaulting act, i.e., the filing of a statement of claim, to be contingent upon sufficient cause not being shown for such failure. However, the corresponding provision of the Act leaves no such scope for the claimant to show sufficient cause for failure to submit such statement of claim leading to the termination of proceedings mandated under section 35 of the Act. The judgment of the Bombay High Court in Wanbury Ltd vs Candid Drug Distributions, Arbitration Petition No. 1461 of 2014 cited by the learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 1, Mr. Mukunda Chandra Debnath as was delivered in light of the fact that the provisions of Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 allowed for sufficient cause to be shown is accordingly distinguished by Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam as not being applicable in the present fact and circumstances. Therefore, this Court finds, since the Act does not permit of sufficient cause to be shown, there is no scope to consider the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 or the aforementioned judgment to be of persuasive nature in providing in any way greater content or the meaning to sections 29 and 35(2(a) of the Act. Furthermore, this Court opines that the entire purpose of the enactment of the Act is to ensure speedy disposal of disputes and, therefore, section 29(1) has been drafted in a manner as leaves no scope for procrastination in such dispute resolution mechanism. It follows that like section (1), section 35(2)(Ka) of the Act is equally of mandatory application permitting an arbitrator to terminate any proceeding where any claimant fails to communicate the statement of claim. Moreover, section 35(5) provides that the arbitration tribunal may order compliance with its orders within such time as deemed fit. Predicated on the golden rule of interpretation of statutes that words prima facie must be given their ordinary meaning, if section 35(2)(a) and section 35(5) are considered together, it would be seen that the former mandates the arbitrator to terminate the proceedings whereas the latter one only gives power to the arbitrator to secure compliance in limited circumstances. This case reveals to this Court the phenomenon also of the double imperative when one considers the provisions of section 35(2)(a) in correlation to section 29(1) of the Act. A perusal of the facts reveals to this Court that by reason of its preoccupation with section 35 the tribunal lost sight of the root provision under section 29 of the Act mandatorily requiring the filing of a claim within the time limit set by the tribunal. There is little doubt in this Court's mind, therefore, that by passing Order No. 6 the sole arbitrator was wholly misguided on these mutually reinforcing clear provisions of applicable law. 

 16. The Petitioner has also challenged the jurisdiction of the arbitrator to pass Order No. 7 dated 31-1-2022 modifying the District Judge's order of status quo dated 21-11-2021 to the extent that the parties shall maintain status quo till 12-2-2022, i.e., until the next hearing date of the arbitration proceedings. It is to be noted that upon rejecting the application for termination of the proceedings the sole arbitrator further fixed 12-2-2022 as the next date of hearing for framing of issues and commencement of hearing and also directed the Petitioner to submit any statement of defense within two weeks. Fundamentally further, as the Petitioner contends, through Order No. 7 dated 31-1-2022 the arbitrator decided to modify a non-existing status quo and directed the parties to maintain such status quo till 12-2-2022. This Court accepts the argument that the arbitrator indeed modified a non-existing status quo order in the facts and directed the parties to maintain the status quo till 12-2-2022. In this regard the sole arbitrator is found to have acted beyond his jurisdiction and acted in violation of section 21(1) of the Act under which a tribunal can only exercise its jurisdiction to issue an interim order only upon an application by the party seeking such an order. In the instant case, the claimant Respondent No. 1 neither submitted any application for status quo nor any application for extension of an order of status quo. As such, this Court finds by passing the order of status quo suo motu and rejecting the application for vacating the order of status quo the sole arbitrator exceeded his authority to do so and, thereby, the said order is found to be manifestly issued beyond jurisdiction. 

 18. The question posed this Court at the outset is, therefore, the extent of its own jurisdiction under section 20 to scrutinize the orders passed by an arbitral tribunal or, as in this case, the sole arbitrator. The word "jurisdiction" has been defined in Stroud's Judicial Dictionary thus: 

 19. The Supreme Court of India, in the case of National Thermal Power Corporation Ltd vs Siemens Atkeingesellschaft as reported in 2007(1) Arb. LR 377 (SC) held that the "expression `jurisdiction' is a word of many hues. Its colour is to be discerned from the setting in which it is used." In Shaqafath Ali Khan and Ors. vs Imdad Jah Bahadur and On as reported in (2009) 5 SCC 162 the Supreme Court of India held that: 

 "A civil revision application although must necessarily having regard to the terminologies used in Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure involve the question of jurisdiction, the question which would arise is as to what are the jurisdictional questions. A jurisdictional question may arise not only when a court acts wholly without jurisdiction but also in a case where jurisdictional errors are committed while exercising jurisdiction. There are various facets of 'jurisdictional errors'. Taking into consideration any irrelevant fact or non-consideration of a. relevant fact would involve jurisdictional issue." 

 20. Furthermore, Section 20(4) provides that, "(4) Unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where any application is pending before the High Court Division under this section, the arbitral tribunal shall continue arbitration proceedings and make an arbitral award". In this regard it is apparent to this Court that sections 20(1) and 20(4) read together permit of the word "jurisdiction" in section 20(1) to refer to a tribunal's jurisdiction not only in regards to its constitution and formation but also to the extent and scope of the tribunal's power of determination. If section 20(1) merely referred to jurisdiction with regards to the formation of a tribunal then the provisions on a tribunal's determinative power in section 20(4) would not have necessarily followed in the scheme of section 20 as a whole. In this regard, it has been affirmed in a myriad of cases including Abu Khair Md. Nazmul Huq and Ors. vs Government of Bangladesh and Ors. as reported in EX/BDHC/0055/2022 that a statute must be read as a whole and not in part. In light of the above, it can be deduced, therefore, that how jurisdiction is exercised is also a matter which definitely falls within an expansive treatment of the word "jurisdiction" in section 20(1) to include the authority and scope of a tribunal to pass any order in the concerned arbitration. 

 any question as to the jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and such a power is an independent power so conferred upon this Court as held in the case of Dhaka North City Corporation vs District Judge, Dhaka reported in (2023] 27 ALR (HCD) 234. Accepted too is the submission that under section 21 of the Act, unlike section 37 of Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, no provision for appeal has been provided against an interim order passed by an arbitral tribunal. Predicated on the above this Court also finds merit in Mr. Alam's submission that the legislature intended, as evident in section 20(4), that section 20 of the Act would enable this Court to examine an order passed by an arbitral tribunal or a sole arbitrator on the question of jurisdiction. Carrying forward such line of reasoning it is this Court's view further that section 20 empowers this Court to examine whether an arbitration tribunal is stepping outside its jurisdiction by passing a patently illegal order and, thereby, causing miscarriage of justice. In this context this Court finds that the word "jurisdiction" is not merely to be taken as being confined to gauging the validity of the arbitration agreement, proper constitution of the arbitral tribunal or whether the matters have been submitted to arbitration in accordance with the arbitration agreement, but also must necessarily extend to cover the determination of the question relating to the scope of jurisdiction and mode of exercise of the same by a tribunal. 

 `But there are many cases where, although the tribunal had jurisdiction to enter on the enquiry, it has done or failed to do something in the course of the enquiry which is of such a nature that its decision is a nullity. It may have given its decision in bad faith. It may have made a decision which it had no power to make. It may have failed in the course of the enquiry to comply with the requirements of natural justice. It may in perfect good faith have misconstrued the provisions giving it power to act so that it failed to deal with the question remitted to it and decided some question which was not remitted to it. It may have refused to take into account something which it was required to take into account. Or it may have based its decision on some matter which, under the provisions setting it up, it had no right to take into account. I do not intend this list to be exhaustive. But if it decides a question remitted to it for decision without committing any of these errors it is as much entitled to decide that question wrongly as it is to decide it rightly." 

 "that the courts had theretofore imposed upon themselves so far as determinations of inferior courts and statutory tribunals were concerned, by drawing esoteric distinctions between errors of law committed by such tribunals that went to their jurisdiction, and errors of law committed by them within their jurisdiction. The breakthrough that the Anisminic case made was the recognition by the majority of this House that if a tribunal whose jurisdiction was limited by statute or subordinate legislation mistook the law applicable to the facts as it had found them, it must have asked itself the wrong question, i.e., one into which it was not empowered to inquire and so had no jurisdiction to determine. Its purported 'determination', not being a 'determination' within the meaning of the empowering legislation, was accordingly a nullity." 

 26. One is reminded too of Lord Lane's evaluation of Anisminic in Pearlman vs Keepers and Governors of Harrow School 119791 QB 56 (CA) that a court as this will always retain the power to quash a decision of an inferior tribunal which has acted in excess of its jurisdiction including a case where, as Lord Reaid emphasized in Anisminic, the purported determination of the tribunal turns out to be a nullity because it cannot be properly called a determination at all. Moreover, Lord Reid in Anisminic made an observation regarding the jurisdiction of the courts to enquire into the decisions made by tribunals. It was held that if there is a provision which is reasonably capable of having two meanings, that meaning shall be taken which preserves the ordinary jurisdiction of the court. As such, this Court finds merit in Mr. Tanjib-ul Alam's submission that when there is a decision of the arbitration tribunal where the tribunal has decided a matter for exceeding its jurisdiction this Court has jurisdiction under section 20 of the Act to adjudicate on that issue. 

 32. Upon a review of the facts and the grounds agitated to support the Petitioner's cause of action, this Court remains satisfied that the sole arbitrator has exceeded his jurisdiction in several ways, namely, by passing an order on an issue even when there was no extant cause of action or dispute, through deciding against the termination of the arbitral proceedings despite being mandated to do so by the Act, extending the order of status quo despite there being no application or prayer from the Respondent No. 1 to do so, and, consequentially, by losing sight of the fact that the current case is not one where specific performance can be ordered. 

 35. Furthermore, the Respondent No. 1 has sought to substantiate its case through attempting to explain the tenor and purport of section 35 by references to ostensibly corresponding provisions of and case law based on the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 in which, however, a significant distinguishing feature has been overlooked by the learned Advocate for the said Respondent. The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides that, "unless otherwise agreed by the parties, where, without showing sufficient cause—(a) the claimant fails to communicate his statement of claim in accordance with sub-section (1) of section 23, the arbitral tribunal shall terminate the proceedings." The words "without showing sufficient cause" mark the point of material difference and deviation between the two aforementioned sections, essentially meaning that the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 provides the arbitrator with a discretion to determine as to whether there was sufficient cause for the failure to submit the statement of claim which is wholly absent in the Act. 

 36. Also the District Judge. Chattogram passed the order dated 21-11-2021 of status quo in the following manner, অত্র আদালতের সালিশী মিছ-১৩৪/২০২১ নং মামলার সালিশী কার্যক্রম বিজ্ঞ জেলাজজ আদালত, ঢাকাতে চলমান থাকায় উক্ত সালিশী কার্যক্রম নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত অত্র সালিশী মিছ মামলায় প্রদত্ত বিগত ৫-৫-২০২১ ইং তারিখের স্থিতাবস্থার আদেশ বলবত থাকিবে। It appears from the order that status quo had to be maintained until the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 134 of 2021 came to an end. The said case was filed by the Respondent No. 1 for the appointment of an arbitrator by reference to section 12 of the Act. However, on account of the supervening development of the Respondent No. 2 entering appearance as the sole arbitrator, the said Miscellaneous Case had, in this Court's opinion, come to be subsumed under the arbitration proceedings presently underway. Under such circumstances, the status quo came to be non-existent and redundant once the sole arbitrator had entered appearance. Moreover, and as otherwise statutorily prescribed, there was no application on behalf of the Respondent No. 1 to modify or extend the order of status quo. Rather, there was an application filed by the Petitioner for vacating the order of status quo which could either be allowed or rejected. However, the Respondent No. 2, sole arbitrator went beyond his jurisdiction by opting instead to modify the said order as operated to the benefit of the Respondent No. 1.
